column1: # lane-bench-classes.tsv — the lane bench's terminal-class map (#812 AC-1, D-5/D-16/D-17).
# slug       A terminal slug of the lean lane's scheduler. The set is DERIVED, not curated:
#            `envfail <slug>` call site out of the shipped orchestrate-lean.sh, plus the one
#            `terminal-vocabulary:` announcement, and requires this file to name exactly that
#            set in BOTH directions. A slug added to the scheduler with no row here reds; a row
#            here naming no live site reds. That is what makes docs/lane-bench.md's claim to
#            cover "the lane's full slug vocabulary" falsifiable rather than prose.
# class      One of approved | paused | no-pr | pr-unapproved | lane-error | unscorable,
#            or `-` for the one announced member that is not a terminal (see below).
# condition  `-` when the class follows from the slug alone; otherwise the extra fact the
#            runner must read to choose, stated as the runner's own predicate.
# THE MAP IS THE EPIC'S, TAKEN VERBATIM (D-16). It is not re-reasoned here, and two of its calls
# would not survive being re-reasoned from the slug text alone: `lane-closed-out` and the whole
# `closeout-*` family are `lane-error` although all four sit downstream of an approve verdict,
# because what the bench measures is a cell that ran to its own terminal, and a cell that could
# not finish its bookkeeping is re-run rather than scored. Changing a class is an epic decision,
# `-` CLASS, ONE ROW. `review-skipped-approved` is announced with the scheduler's
# `terminal-vocabulary:` prefix but no `terminal` call carries it: the run says it and falls into
# the close-out, which terminals under another slug. No results row can hold it. It is listed so
# the completeness guard can tell an announced member from a missing one (D-17).
# WHO READS THIS. Both subcommands. `lane-bench.sh run` derives a cell's class from its terminal
# slug here — and chooses between a slug's two rows by the PAIR OF CLASSES they offer, never by
# the slug: `{paused, no-pr}` is decided by a milestone-1 pause-and-ask row in the progress record,
# `{pr-unapproved, no-pr}` by PR presence on the lane branch. A slug this file does not list, or a
# pair the runner does not model, is `lane-error` — a cell whose class the bench cannot read is
# re-run rather than guessed at. The condition column below stays prose for the reader; the code
# reads the classes. `lane-bench.sh score` reads this file for exactly one thing — validating the
# `unscorable` class it writes when a cell cannot be scored.
